title: First, understanding
hookLine: the first request of the Amidah is for knowledge

lines: WHAT WOULD YOU ASK FOR FIRST?
cards: If you were handed a list of everything you could ask for, in order, what would go first? Money, if this month is tight. Health, if the test results aren't back.
A partner, a job, for the noise to stop. The weekday Amidah has a run of requests in its middle, and it chooses the first one carefully. Not bread.
Not healing. Not peace. Something you might not have thought to ask for at all.

teach.b: The fourth blessing, the first request, begins: You graciously give a person knowledge, and teach human beings understanding. Then it asks for three things: de'ah, knowledge; binah, understanding; and haskel, insight.
It ends: blessed are You, who graciously gives knowledge. Binah is the word to hold. Some teachers hear in it the word bein, between: discerning means telling one thing from another.
When King Solomon is told he can ask for anything, he asks, in the old Jewish translation, "Give Thy servant therefore an understanding heart", to tell good from bad. Why put it first?
The Talmud, in Berakhot 33a, says: great is knowledge, for it was placed at the start of the weekday blessings.

And on Saturday night, when Shabbat ends, a paragraph of havdalah, separation between holy time and ordinary time, is added right here. Why here? Because if there's no understanding, how can there be distinguishing?
You can't separate Shabbat from Sunday without the capacity to tell them apart.
Before you ask for anything else, you ask to know what to ask for: before healing, before money, before peace, the ability to see your own situation clearly.
Solomon could have asked for riches.
He asked for a heart that could tell good from bad, and the Amidah opens its requests the same way.

how: Atah chonen, the request for knowledge, is the fourth blessing of the weekday Amidah; on Saturday night, at the evening service, the havdalah paragraph Atah chonantanu is added inside it.

o: understanding: the power to tell one thing from another
knowledge: memorizing the texts word for word
faith: trusting God without asking any questions

games.q: inside the first request — tap the pairs.

s: the first request of the Amidah is for daily bread
it's for knowledge, understanding and insight.
havdalah is added to this blessing on Saturday night
without understanding, the Talmud asks, how can there be distinguishing?
Solomon asked for an understanding heart
offered anything, he asked for understanding, to tell good from bad.

games.q: the rabbis are deciding where to put the prayer that separates Shabbat from the week on Saturday night. where does it go?
o: at the very end of the service.
games.why: Berakhot 33a: if there's no understanding, how can there be distinguishing? so havdalah goes into the blessing for knowledge.

practice: Bring to mind one situation you don't fully understand: a person who keeps reacting in a way you can't make sense of, a choice you've been circling for weeks, your own mood lately.
Don't try to solve it; just ask, in whatever way is yours, help me see this clearly. If you pray, you can ask God for binah, then sit with the question open.

wordCard.voice: Binah. Understanding: the power to tell one thing from another. The first request of the weekday Amidah. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: understanding. some teachers hear bein, between, in it: discerning one thing from another.

carryVoice: Your line: an understanding heart. A week that opened your lips, prayed quietly with Hannah, named the ancestors, supported the falling, waited for rain, rose with the angels, and finally began to ask. That's day five hundred eighty-one.
